pr.title: Add `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]` for standard library UB checks
pr.description:
should help with #121110 and also with #120848

Because the MIR inliner cannot know whether the checks are enabled or not, so inlining is an unnecessary compile time pessimization when debug assertions are disabled. LLVM knows whether they are enabled or not, so it can optimize accordingly without wasting time.

r? @saethlin
pr.author: Noratrieb

processing.reason: The PR's historical change is an inliner policy guard, not a value-changing rewrite. `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]` only prevents the MIR `Inline` pass from inlining an otherwise inline-eligible callee; the corrected behavior leaves `_1 = callee() -> [return: bb1, unwind ...]` in MIR, while the historically "wrong" behavior inlines the same call. Inlining is semantics-preserving: both `callee()` (an empty function, per tests/mir-opt/inline/rustc_no_mir_inline.rs) and its inlined body produce identical observable results. The PR itself describes the problem as a "compile time pessimization when debug assertions are disabled," explicitly noting LLVM can still optimize/deleting the check. Thus there is no source-grounded original/transformed pair whose repeated defined executions produce different numeric/boolean/character values. Constructing one would require adding an unrelated return-value or side-effect change not justified by the patch, which the task forbids. The only real regression evidence is MIR shape/compile-time, not runtime semantics.

analysis.originalLogic: The MIR `Inline` pass decides whether to inline a callee based on inline hints and inlinability. In `library/core/src/intrinsics.rs`, `assert_unsafe_precondition!` previously controlled its `precondition_check` function with `#[cfg_attr(debug_assertions, inline(always))]` and `#[cfg_attr(not(debug_assertions), inline(never))]`, so the MIR inliner had no way to know that the check is disabled at compile time in release builds.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: A MIR inliner that ignores the new exclusion attribute will inline a callee annotated `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]` into its caller whenever the callee is otherwise inline-eligible (for example because it also has `#[inline]`). For standard-library UB checks this is a compile-time pessimization: the inliner cannot see whether the `debug_assertions`-guarded check will codegen to `false`, so it may inline work that LLVM would simply delete. The corrected transformation rejects such callees at the start of the inline decision, leaving the call intact in MIR, while `#[inline]` still allows LLVM/codegen to inline it when useful.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust MIR processed by the MIR `Inline` pass with `-Zmir-opt-level=2 -Zinline-mir`, for callees carrying the internal `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]` attribute (and typically `#[inline]`). The motivating domain is standard-library `assert_unsafe_precondition!`/`precondition_check` UB checks when debug assertions are disabled, across both `panic-abort` and `panic-unwind` strategies.
analysis.summary: Historical PR adds an internal `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]` attribute and makes the MIR `Inline` pass refuse to inline callees carrying it, so standard-library UB precondition checks remain callable in MIR and can be evaluated/deleted by LLVM instead of wasting MIR inliner compile time when debug assertions are off. The attribute intentionally does not affect codegen inlining.
analysis.trigger: The `Inline` pass considers a callsite whose callee has `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]`. The new guard checks the callee def-id before other inline heuristics and returns `Err("#[rustc_no_mir_inline]")`, so the call is not inlined at MIR level.
preconditions: The MIR inliner is active, e.g. `-Zmir-opt-level=2 -Zinline-mir`.
The callee is annotated with the builtin `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]` attribute.
The attribute is registered as a builtin and the test crate enables `#![feature(rustc_attrs)]`.
For the standard-library use case, the precondition check is built without bootstrap and with debug assertions disabled.
pitfalls: `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]` only blocks the MIR inliner; it does not forbid LLVM or codegen from inlining the function (`#[inline]` may still be present). Do not test it as equivalent to `#[inline(never)]`.
The correct MIR expectation for an excluded callee is that the call remains, e.g. `_1 = callee() -> [return: bb1, unwind unreachable];`, in both the before-Inline and after-Inline dumps.
The guard must run before other inline decisions; otherwise an otherwise-eligible callee could still be inlined.
Panic strategy changes only the unwind action in the test MIR, so the test uses `EMIT_MIR_FOR_EACH_PANIC_STRATEGY` and must cover both panic-abort and panic-unwind expectations.
The old `inline(always)`/`inline(never)` behavior is retained only for `cfg(bootstrap)`; it is not the steady-state mechanism being tested.
Do not infer correctness from a retained test name or comment; compare the actual MIR call in the decoded revisions.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a `tests/mir-opt/inline/rustc_no_mir_inline.rs` MIR-opt test with `#![crate_type = "lib"]`, `#![feature(rustc_attrs)]`, compile flags `-Zmir-opt-level=2 -Zinline-mir`, a `#[inline] #[rustc_no_mir_inline] pub fn callee() {}`, and a `caller()` that invokes it. Emit the `Inline` diff and the `PreCodegen.after` MIR, checking that `caller` still contains `callee()`. Build two otherwise-identical programs differing only in whether the callee carries `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]`: the annotated callee must survive the Inline pass, while the unannotated eligible callee may be inlined. Run under both panic strategies via `EMIT_MIR_FOR_EACH_PANIC_STRATEGY`.
evidence: Add `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]` for standard library UB checks
Because the MIR inliner cannot know whether the checks are enabled or not, so inlining is an unnecessary compile time pessimization when debug assertions are disabled.
LLVM knows whether they are enabled or not, so it can optimize accordingly without wasting time.
"#[rustc_no_mir_inline] prevents the MIR inliner from inlining a function while not affecting codegen"
// This check is inlineable, but not by the MIR inliner.
// LLVM on the other hand sees the constant branch, so if it's `false`, it can immediately delete it without
// inlining the check. If it's `true`, it can inline it and get significantly better performance.
